Common flags: `-i` (case-insensitive), `-n` (show line numbers), `-l` (show only filenames), `-c` (count matches), `-v` (invert — show non-matching lines), `-E` (extended regex). `grep -rn 'ERROR' /var/log/ | tail -50`

questions.question: What is the purpose of `cron` and what does `0 2 * * *` mean in a crontab?

options.text: cron is a process manager; `0 2 * * *` means every 2 seconds
cron is a task scheduler; `0 2 * * *` means every day at 2:00 AM
cron is a log rotator; `0 2 * * *` means twice daily at midnight
cron is a backup tool; `0 2 * * *` means every 2 minutes

questions.explanation: Cron runs scheduled commands. Crontab format: `minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week command`. `0 2 * * *` = minute 0, hour 2, every day, every month, every weekday → daily at 02:00. Use `crontab -e` to edit, `crontab -l` to list. `@daily`, `@weekly` are shorthand aliases.
questions.codeSnippet:
# minute hour dom month dow command
0 2 * * *    /usr/bin/backup.sh
*/15 * * * * /usr/bin/healthcheck.sh  # Every 15 min
0 0 1 * *    /usr/bin/monthly.sh      # First of month

questions.question: What is the difference between `kill`, `kill -9`, and `killall`?

options.text: `kill` deletes a process; `kill -9` pauses it; `killall` resumes it
`kill PID` sends SIGTERM (graceful); `kill -9 PID` sends SIGKILL (force); `killall name` sends a signal to all processes with that name
`kill -9` is safer than `kill`; `killall` only works as root
All three do the same thing — just different syntax

questions.explanation: `kill PID` sends SIGTERM (15) — process can catch it and shut down gracefully. `kill -9 PID` sends SIGKILL — uncatchable, immediate termination, risk of data corruption. `killall nginx` sends SIGTERM to all processes named nginx. `pkill -f pattern` kills by command pattern. Always try SIGTERM first.

questions.question: What does `netstat -tlnp` or `ss -tlnp` show?

options.text: All network traffic in real-time
All TCP listening ports with the PID/program name bound to them
The routing table of the host
Network interface statistics and bandwidth usage

questions.explanation: `ss -tlnp` (modern replacement for netstat): `-t` TCP, `-l` listening only, `-n` numeric (no DNS lookup), `-p` show process. Shows which ports are open and which process owns them. Useful for: confirming your app started on the right port, finding port conflicts, security auditing of exposed services.

questions.question: What is `systemd` and how do you manage services with it?

options.text: systemd is a file synchronization daemon; services are managed with `sync` command
systemd is the init system and service manager on most modern Linux distros; services are managed with `systemctl start/stop/enable/disable/status`
systemd is a package manager; services are installed with `systemd install`
systemd is a log viewer; services emit logs to systemd with syslog

questions.explanation: systemd is PID 1 on most modern Linux systems (Ubuntu 16+, RHEL 7+, Debian 8+). Key commands: `systemctl start nginx`, `systemctl stop nginx`, `systemctl restart nginx`, `systemctl enable nginx` (start at boot), `systemctl status nginx` (view state + recent logs), `journalctl -u nginx -f` (follow logs).

questions.question: What does `df -h` vs `du -sh *` tell you?

options.text: Both show disk usage — `df` is faster, `du` is more accurate
`df -h` shows filesystem disk space usage (free/used per partition); `du -sh *` shows disk usage of each item in the current directory
`df` shows disk failures; `du` shows disk utilization per process
`df -h` shows RAM usage; `du -sh *` shows disk usage

questions.explanation: `df -h` (disk free): shows filesystem-level free/used space per mounted partition. `-h` = human-readable. `du -sh *` (disk usage): shows how much space each file/directory in the current path uses. `-s` = summary (don't recurse into dirs), `-h` = human-readable. Use `du -sh * | sort -rh | head -10` to find the biggest directories.

questions.question: What is `ssh-keygen` and what does passwordless SSH authentication look like?

options.text: ssh-keygen generates passwords for SSH servers
ssh-keygen generates a key pair; the public key is added to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server; private key stays on the client — no password needed
ssh-keygen generates a session token that expires in 24 hours
Passwordless SSH is not possible; a password is always required

questions.explanation: Flow: `ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C 'mykey'` creates `id_ed25519` (private, keep secret) and `id_ed25519.pub` (public). Copy public key to server: `ssh-copy-id user@server` (appends to `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`). SSH challenges the client to prove they have the private key without sending it over the network.

questions.question: What does `awk '{print $2}' file.txt` do?

options.text: Prints the second line of the file
Prints the second field (column) of each line, using whitespace as the default delimiter
Adds a second copy of each line to the output
Skips the first line and prints all remaining lines

questions.explanation: `awk` is a text processing tool. `$1`, `$2`, `$NF` refer to fields. Default field separator is whitespace. Example: `ps aux | awk '{print $1, $2, $11}'` prints user, PID, and command. `awk -F: '{print $1}' /etc/passwd` prints usernames (`:` delimiter). `awk '/pattern/ {print $0}'` prints matching lines.

questions.question: What is a bash `set -euo pipefail` and why do scripts use it?

options.text: It enables debug mode, printing every command before execution
`-e` exits on error, `-u` errors on unset variables, `-o pipefail` causes pipes to fail if any command fails — makes scripts fail fast and predictably
It enables strict mode that prevents any command from running as root
It configures the shell to use UTC timezone for all date commands

questions.explanation: Without `set -e`, a script continues after a failed command. Without `-u`, using an unset variable silently substitutes empty string (data loss risk). Without `pipefail`, `failing-command | grep x` succeeds because grep finds nothing, hiding the upstream failure. Together, these flags catch errors early in CI scripts.
questions.codeSnippet:
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

DEPLOY_ENV="${DEPLOY_ENV}"  # Fails if DEPLOY_ENV not set
docker build -t myapp .
docker push myapp            # Script stops here if this fails

questions.question: What is `tail -f /var/log/app.log` used for?

options.text: Shows the first 10 lines of the log file
Follows the log file in real-time, printing new lines as they are written
Deletes the last 10 lines from the log file
Compresses the log file using the f (fast) algorithm

questions.explanation: `tail -f` (follow) keeps the file open and prints new lines as they appear — essential for live log monitoring. `-n 100 -f` shows last 100 lines then follows. Modern alternative: `journalctl -u myservice -f` for systemd services. `tail -f` works on any file including Docker log files.

questions.question: What is the Linux `/proc` filesystem?

options.text: A filesystem for storing application configuration files
A virtual filesystem exposing kernel and process information as files — reading `/proc/PID/status` gives process info without any syscall overhead
A protected filesystem only accessible by root
A filesystem for storing process core dumps

questions.explanation: The `/proc` filesystem is a virtual FS that exists only in memory. It provides a window into kernel state: `/proc/cpuinfo` (CPU info), `/proc/meminfo` (RAM usage), `/proc/PID/fd` (open file descriptors), `/proc/PID/environ` (environment variables), `/proc/net/tcp` (TCP connections). Tools like `ps`, `top`, `ss` read from `/proc`.

questions.question: What does `curl -I https://example.com` do?

options.text: Downloads the page content of example.com
Sends an HTTP HEAD request and shows only the response headers
Tests if port 443 is open on example.com
Prints information about the curl binary itself

questions.explanation: `-I` (or `--head`) sends HTTP HEAD — gets only headers, no body. Useful for checking status codes, content-type, server version, cache headers, and redirect chains without downloading content. `curl -IL` follows redirects. For full request/response debugging: `curl -v https://example.com`.

questions.question: What is `sudo` and what is the difference between `sudo command` and `su -`?

options.text: `sudo` runs one command as root; `su -` opens a full root shell — both require the root password
`sudo command` runs one command as root using YOUR password; `su -` switches to the root user entirely using the root password
`sudo` is for installing packages; `su` is for service management
They are identical — `sudo` is just shorthand for `su -c`

questions.explanation: `sudo` (Superuser Do) elevates one command using your own password, governed by `/etc/sudoers`. It's audited (logged to syslog). `su -` starts a full root login shell — requires knowing the root password (disabled on Ubuntu by default). `sudo -i` or `sudo su -` gives a root shell using sudo policy.

questions.question: What is a Linux signal and what are the most important ones to know?

options.text: Signals are kernel notifications sent to processes to request an action or notify of an event
Signals are network packets sent between Linux servers
Signals are log messages written to /var/log/signals
Signals are CPU interrupts that pause process execution

questions.explanation: Key signals: SIGTERM (15) — graceful shutdown request, can be caught; SIGKILL (9) — immediate kill, cannot be caught or ignored; SIGHUP (1) — traditionally reloads config (nginx: `kill -HUP PID`); SIGINT (2) — Ctrl+C; SIGQUIT (3) — Ctrl+\, creates core dump; SIGUSR1/SIGUSR2 — user-defined, many apps use for log rotation.

questions.question: What is the difference between a process and a thread in Linux?

options.text: Processes share memory; threads have separate memory spaces
A process has its own memory space (virtual address space); threads within a process share the same memory space but have separate execution stacks
Threads are managed by the kernel; processes are managed by the application
Processes run in parallel; threads run sequentially

questions.explanation: Processes are independent units with separate address spaces — inter-process communication requires IPC mechanisms (pipes, sockets, shared memory). Threads within a process share the same virtual memory, file descriptors, and signal handlers, but each has its own stack and registers. In Linux, both are created with `clone()` syscall with different flags.

questions.question: What is `strace` and when would you use it?

options.text: strace tracks network connections made by a process
strace intercepts and logs system calls made by a process — used for debugging mysterious crashes, permission errors, or to understand what files/sockets a process accesses
strace is a CPU performance profiler
strace traces bash script execution line by line

questions.explanation: `strace -p PID` attaches to a running process and logs every syscall (open, read, write, connect, execve...). `strace -e trace=file,network mycommand` filters to file and network calls. Use when: app fails silently, you suspect a permission issue, you need to find what config file is being read, or debugging a binary you don't have source for.

questions.question: What is an environment variable and how do you make one persist across sessions?

options.text: Environment variables exist only in memory; to persist, add `export VAR=value` to ~/.bashrc or ~/.bash_profile
All environment variables persist automatically between sessions
Environment variables are stored in /etc/environment and automatically apply to all users
Use `setenv VAR value` to make a variable persistent

questions.explanation: Environment variables set with `export VAR=value` exist only for the current session and child processes. For persistence: add to `~/.bashrc` (bash interactive shells), `~/.bash_profile` (bash login shells), or `/etc/environment` (system-wide). `source ~/.bashrc` reloads without restarting the shell.
questions.codeSnippet:
# Temporary (current session only)
export NODE_ENV=production

# Persistent — add to ~/.bashrc
echo 'export NODE_ENV=production' >> ~/.bashrc
source ~/.bashrc

questions.question: What does `|` (pipe) do in Linux shell commands?

options.text: Pipes write output to a file
Pipes connect the stdout of one command to the stdin of the next, enabling command chaining
Pipes run two commands simultaneously in background
Pipes redirect stderr to /dev/null

questions.explanation: The pipe `|` passes stdout of the left command as stdin to the right command. This enables the Unix philosophy of small tools that do one thing well, composed together. Example: `ps aux | grep nginx | awk '{print $2}' | xargs kill` — find nginx PIDs and kill them. Pipes work in memory with no temp files.
questions.codeSnippet:
# Find top 5 memory-consuming processes
ps aux | sort -rk 4 | head -5

# Count error lines in logs
grep 'ERROR' app.log | wc -l

# Find and kill a process
pgrep nginx | xargs kill -9

questions.question: What does `find /var/log -name '*.log' -mtime +7 -delete` do?

options.text: Finds log files modified in the last 7 days and deletes them
Finds .log files in /var/log that were last modified more than 7 days ago and deletes them
Finds files larger than 7MB and moves them to /var/log
Counts all log files older than 7 minutes

questions.explanation: `find` with `-mtime +7` means 'modified more than 7 days ago' (`+` means older, `-` means newer). `-name '*.log'` filters by filename pattern. `-delete` deletes matching files (use without `-delete` first to preview). Commonly used in cron for log cleanup. `-exec rm {} \;` is the alternative to `-delete`.

questions.question: What is `lsof` and how is it useful?

options.text: lsof lists all open file systems
lsof (list open files) shows all files opened by processes — including network sockets, so `lsof -i :3000` shows what's using port 3000
lsof lists recently deleted files that can be recovered
lsof is a log viewer for system open file events

questions.explanation: `lsof -i :3000` shows what process has port 3000 open. `lsof -p PID` shows all files/sockets a process has open. `lsof /path/to/file` shows which process has a file open (useful when you can't delete a file that's 'in use'). In Linux, everything is a file — including network connections.

questions.question: What are Linux namespaces and cgroups, and how do they relate to containers?

options.text: Namespaces are file permission groups; cgroups are network isolation zones
Namespaces provide isolation of system resources (PID, network, filesystem, users); cgroups limit resource usage (CPU, memory). Together they are the kernel features that containers are built on
They are Linux kernel modules for hypervisor virtualization
Namespaces are for user accounts; cgroups manage process groups

questions.explanation: Linux namespaces isolate a process's view of the system: PID namespace (own PID 1), network namespace (own network stack), mount namespace (own filesystem view), UTS namespace (own hostname), IPC namespace. Cgroups (control groups) limit and account for resource usage. Docker uses both: namespaces for isolation, cgroups for resource limits — containers are just processes with restricted views.

questions.question: What are the three pillars of observability?

options.text: Monitoring, alerting, and dashboards
Metrics, logs, and traces
CPU, memory, and disk
Uptime, latency, and errors

questions.explanation: The three pillars: Metrics (numeric measurements over time — CPU%, request count, error rate), Logs (timestamped records of discrete events), and Traces (records of a request's journey through distributed services). Together they let you understand the state of a system and why it behaves the way it does.

questions.question: What is the difference between monitoring and observability?

options.text: Monitoring is for infrastructure; observability is for application code
Monitoring tells you when something is wrong (alerting on known failure modes); observability lets you understand WHY by exploring data you didn't anticipate needing
Observability is the old term; monitoring is the modern replacement
They are the same concept with different names

questions.explanation: Monitoring: you know what to watch (CPU > 90%, error rate > 1%), and you alert when thresholds are breached — good for known problems. Observability: ability to answer arbitrary questions about system state from its outputs (metrics + logs + traces) — essential for debugging unknown unknowns in complex distributed systems.

questions.question: What is Prometheus and how does it collect metrics?

options.text: Prometheus is a log aggregation tool that receives pushed logs
Prometheus is an open-source monitoring system that scrapes (pulls) metrics from instrumented targets at regular intervals and stores them in a time-series database
Prometheus is a distributed tracing system
Prometheus is an alerting tool that integrates with Grafana

questions.explanation: Prometheus uses a pull model: it scrapes HTTP endpoints (typically `/metrics`) on configured targets at regular intervals (default 15s). Applications expose metrics in Prometheus format via client libraries (prom-client for Node.js). Prometheus stores metrics as time-series data and provides PromQL for querying. Alertmanager handles alert routing.

questions.question: What is Grafana and how does it relate to Prometheus?

options.text: Grafana is a replacement for Prometheus with built-in visualization
Grafana is a visualization and dashboarding platform that queries data sources (Prometheus, Loki, CloudWatch, Elasticsearch) and displays them as dashboards
Grafana stores metrics data; Prometheus visualizes them
Grafana is a log aggregation tool that feeds data into Prometheus

questions.explanation: Prometheus stores and queries metrics. Grafana visualizes them. Grafana connects to Prometheus as a data source, and you build dashboards with panels using PromQL queries. The Prometheus+Grafana stack is standard for self-hosted monitoring. Grafana also supports Loki (logs), Tempo (traces), and 50+ other data sources.

questions.question: What is a Service Level Objective (SLO) and how does it differ from an SLA?

options.text: SLO is internal reliability target; SLA is the legal contract with customers specifying the consequences of not meeting the SLO
SLA is the internal target; SLO is the customer-facing contract
They are the same thing — SLO is the acronym used by engineers, SLA by managers
SLO is for infrastructure; SLA is for application performance

questions.explanation: SLI (Service Level Indicator): a metric measuring service behavior (success rate, latency). SLO: internal reliability target (e.g., 99.9% success rate). SLA: legal contract promising customers a reliability level, with penalties (refunds, credits) if breached. SLOs should be tighter than SLAs — you want to catch and fix problems before SLA penalties kick in.

questions.question: What is an error budget and how is it used in SRE?

options.text: A budget allocated to the engineering team for fixing bugs
The acceptable amount of downtime/errors derived from an SLO — if error budget is exhausted, reliability work takes priority over feature development
The maximum number of error logs before an alert fires
A cost estimate for incident response

questions.explanation: If your SLO is 99.9% uptime, your error budget is 0.1% (about 8.7 hours/year). If you're burning budget faster than allowed, you slow feature releases and invest in reliability. If budget is healthy, you can take more deployment risks. Error budgets make reliability a shared engineering goal, not just an ops concern.

questions.question: What is the ELK/EFK stack?

options.text: A CI/CD stack: Environment, Linting, and Kubernetes
ELK: Elasticsearch (storage/search), Logstash/Fluentd (collection/processing), Kibana (visualization) — a centralized log management platform
A monitoring stack: Events, Logs, and Kubernetes
ELK is a Grafana plugin for log visualization

questions.explanation: ELK: Elasticsearch stores and indexes logs, Logstash collects and transforms logs, Kibana visualizes logs with search and dashboards. EFK replaces Logstash with Fluentd (lighter, Kubernetes-native). Common flow: app → Fluentd DaemonSet → Elasticsearch → Kibana. OpenSearch is the AWS fork of Elasticsearch used in managed services.

questions.question: What is distributed tracing and what problem does it solve?

options.text: Distributed tracing logs all database queries across a cluster
Distributed tracing follows a request across multiple services, recording timing and context at each hop — making it possible to find bottlenecks or failures in microservices architectures
Distributed tracing monitors network packet routes between servers
Distributed tracing is a debugging tool for multithreaded applications

questions.explanation: In a microservices architecture, a single user request touches 10+ services. When it's slow or fails, which service is the culprit? Distributed tracing assigns each request a unique trace ID and records spans (timed operations) at each service. Tools: Jaeger, Zipkin, AWS X-Ray, Honeycomb. Standard protocol: OpenTelemetry.

questions.question: What is OpenTelemetry (OTel)?

options.text: A cloud provider for managed monitoring services
A vendor-neutral, open-source observability framework providing APIs, SDKs, and collectors for generating and exporting metrics, logs, and traces
A Prometheus-compatible metrics format for Kubernetes
A log format standard created by Elasticsearch

questions.explanation: OpenTelemetry (CNCF project) standardizes how telemetry data is generated, collected, and exported. Instrument your code once with OTel SDKs, then export to any backend (Jaeger, Datadog, Honeycomb, Prometheus, Grafana Tempo) by changing the exporter config. Avoids vendor lock-in in your instrumentation code.

questions.question: What are the four golden signals of monitoring?

options.text: CPU, Memory, Disk, Network
Latency, Traffic, Errors, and Saturation
Uptime, Throughput, Alerts, and Dashboards
Requests, Response time, Error logs, and Cache hits

questions.explanation: Google SRE book's four golden signals: Latency (how long requests take — separate successful vs error latency), Traffic (requests per second), Errors (failed requests), Saturation (how full the service is — queue depth, CPU%). These four metrics, if all healthy, strongly suggest the service is functioning correctly.

questions.question: What is the difference between a gauge, counter, and histogram in Prometheus?

options.text: Gauge is for latency, counter is for errors, histogram is for uptime
Counter: monotonically increasing value (total requests); Gauge: value that goes up and down (current memory); Histogram: samples observations in configurable buckets (request duration distribution)
They are three names for the same metric type
Gauges and counters are for infrastructure; histograms are for business metrics

questions.explanation: Counter: only increases (resets on restart), e.g., `http_requests_total`. Query with `rate()`. Gauge: can go up and down, e.g., `memory_usage_bytes`, `active_connections`. Histogram: counts observations in buckets, calculates sum and count — use for latency percentiles (`histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(http_duration_bucket[5m]))`). Summary: similar to histogram but calculates quantiles client-side.

questions.question: What is alert fatigue and how do you prevent it?

options.text: Alert fatigue is when monitoring tools slow down due to too many metrics

Alert fatigue is when on-call engineers become desensitized to alerts because too many are noisy or non-actionable — prevented by alerting only on symptoms, not causes, and requiring every alert to be actionable
Alert fatigue is a CPU issue caused by too many alert checks
Alert fatigue only affects large organizations with 100+ engineers

questions.explanation: Alert fatigue: when engineers receive too many alerts, they start ignoring them — including real incidents. Prevention: (1) Alert on symptoms (user-visible impact) not causes. (2) Every alert must be actionable — if the response is 'do nothing', delete the alert. (3) Set appropriate thresholds. (4) Use SLO-based alerting (burn rate). (5) Regularly review and prune alert rules.

questions.question: What is a runbook and why is it important for incident response?

options.text: A runbook is a script that automatically resolves incidents
A runbook is a documented procedure for responding to a specific alert or incident — reducing time-to-resolve and enabling less experienced engineers to handle incidents
A runbook is a log file of all commands run during an incident
A runbook is a Kubernetes resource for automated recovery

questions.explanation: A runbook links directly from an alert and documents: what this alert means, who to escalate to, step-by-step diagnostic commands, common causes and resolutions, and rollback procedures. Reduces MTTR (Mean Time to Resolve) significantly. Good runbooks enable on-call rotation beyond the original developer.

questions.question: What is a postmortem (or incident review) in SRE/DevOps?

options.text: A process for firing engineers who caused an outage
A blameless document written after an incident that analyzes root causes, contributing factors, and action items to prevent recurrence
A final technical audit before a service is deprecated
A quarterly performance review of the infrastructure

questions.explanation: Postmortems are blameless — the goal is learning, not blame. Structure: incident timeline, impact, root cause analysis (5 whys), contributing factors, and action items with owners and due dates. Blamelessness is critical: if engineers fear punishment, they hide problems and incidents go unlearned from. Pioneered by Google SRE.

questions.question: What is PromQL `rate()` and when should you use it vs `increase()`?

options.text: rate() is for gauges; increase() is for counters
rate() calculates the per-second rate of a counter over a time window; increase() calculates the total increase over the window — use rate() for dashboards, increase() for 'how many in this window'
They are identical — rate() = increase() / 60
rate() is deprecated; use increase() instead

questions.explanation: `rate(http_requests_total[5m])` gives requests per second averaged over the last 5 minutes — good for throughput graphs and alert rules (rate > threshold). `increase(http_requests_total[5m])` gives total requests in 5 minutes — good for 'how many errors happened'. Both handle counter resets gracefully. Never use `rate()` on gauges.
questions.codeSnippet:
# Requests per second (last 5 min average)
rate(http_requests_total[5m])

# Error rate percentage
rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m])
/ rate(http_requests_total[5m]) * 100

# Total errors in last hour
increase(http_errors_total[1h])

questions.question: What is a health check endpoint and what should it return?

options.text: A health check should return the server's CPU and memory usage

A health check endpoint (e.g., /health or /ready) returns the service's operational status — typically a JSON with status and HTTP 200 if healthy, 5xx if not — used by load balancers, Kubernetes, and monitoring
A health check should return the application version and git SHA
Health check endpoints should require authentication to prevent abuse

questions.explanation: Health checks validate that the service can handle requests. Liveness check: is the process alive? (return 200). Readiness check: can it serve traffic? (check database connectivity, cache, etc. — return 503 if not ready). Kubernetes uses these for traffic routing and restart decisions. Load balancers remove unhealthy backends.

questions.question: What is log aggregation and why is it important in distributed systems?

options.text: Log aggregation compresses log files to save disk space
Log aggregation collects logs from all services/instances into a central searchable store — essential when debugging issues that span multiple services or when running many container instances
Log aggregation is a security feature that masks sensitive data in logs
Log aggregation is only needed for apps generating more than 1GB of logs per day

questions.explanation: With 50 microservices each running 3 instances = 150 log streams. Without aggregation, debugging requires SSHing into each instance. Centralized logging (ELK, Loki, CloudWatch Logs) collects all logs and enables: cross-service correlation by trace ID, full-text search, alerting on log patterns, and retention policies.

questions.question: What is SLO-based alerting (burn rate alerting)?

options.text: Alerting when CPU burns above 90% for more than 5 minutes
Alerting when the error budget is being consumed faster than the SLO allows — e.g., alert if the error rate over 1 hour would exhaust the monthly budget in 2 days
Burning through alert budget — the maximum number of alerts per month
SLO-based alerting only works with Prometheus

questions.explanation: Burn rate alerting alerts on how fast you're consuming your error budget, not absolute thresholds. A 1-hour 14x burn rate means you'd exhaust a 30-day monthly budget in ~2 days — that's page-worthy. A 6-hour 3x burn rate means budget depletes in 10 days — ticket-worthy but not paging. This reduces false positives vs simple threshold alerts.

questions.question: What is Grafana Loki and how does it differ from Elasticsearch?

options.text: Loki is a metrics tool; Elasticsearch is a log tool
Loki indexes only log metadata (labels), not the full text — making it cheaper to operate. Elasticsearch indexes full log content for fast full-text search but is resource-intensive
Loki is cloud-only; Elasticsearch is self-hosted only
They are identical — Loki is just the Grafana-branded version of Elasticsearch

questions.explanation: Loki (from Grafana Labs) is 'Prometheus, but for logs'. It uses the same label system as Prometheus and stores log streams indexed only by labels (app, env, pod). Log content is stored compressed and not indexed — searches are grep-like over the matching streams. Much cheaper than Elasticsearch. Trade-off: no full-text search — queries must filter by label first.

questions.question: What is a Service Mesh (e.g., Istio, Linkerd) and what observability features does it provide?

options.text: A service mesh is a Kubernetes networking plugin that replaces CoreDNS
A service mesh is an infrastructure layer that intercepts all service-to-service traffic via sidecar proxies, providing automatic metrics, traces, mTLS, and traffic management without code changes
A service mesh is a monitoring tool specifically for databases
A service mesh is the network topology diagram of a microservices application

questions.explanation: A service mesh (Istio, Linkerd, Consul Connect) deploys a sidecar proxy (Envoy) alongside each service pod. The proxy intercepts all inbound/outbound traffic, providing: automatic L7 metrics (success rate, latency, throughput) for every service pair, distributed traces, mTLS for all service communication, and traffic management (canary, circuit breaking, retries) — all without app code changes.

questions.question: What are structured logs and why are they preferred over unstructured logs?

options.text: Structured logs use XML format; unstructured logs use plain text
Structured logs (JSON, key=value) include consistent fields making them machine-parseable and searchable by field; unstructured logs are free-form text requiring regex to extract fields
Structured logs are compressed; unstructured logs are not
Structured logs are for production; unstructured logs are for development

questions.explanation: Unstructured: `ERROR 2024-01-15 Database connection failed for user john after 3 attempts`. Structured: `{"level":"error","timestamp":"2024-01-15","message":"Database connection failed","user":"john","attempts":3}`. Structured logs enable: filtering by field (all errors for user 'john'), aggregation (count by error type), alerting on specific fields, and correlation by trace_id — much more powerful for debugging.

questions.question: What is MTTR (Mean Time to Recovery) and what factors affect it?

options.text: Mean Time to Request — the average time an HTTP request takes
Mean Time to Recovery — the average time from incident detection to service restoration; affected by detection speed, runbook quality, deployment rollback speed, and on-call response time
Mean Time to Release — the average time from code commit to production
Mean Time to Restart — the average time for servers to reboot

questions.explanation: MTTR = average time from incident start to resolution. Factors: (1) Detection: how quickly alerts fire (alert thresholds, synthetic monitoring). (2) Diagnosis: observability quality, runbooks. (3) Resolution: rollback automation, deployment pipeline speed. (4) Response: on-call rotations, escalation policies. Elite teams target MTTR < 1 hour.

questions.question: What is synthetic monitoring?

options.text: Monitoring using AI-generated fake metrics to simulate load
Proactively testing a service by running automated scripts (simulated user journeys) on a schedule — detecting issues before real users do
Monitoring that generates synthetic test data for load testing
Monitoring that uses machine learning to predict future failures

questions.explanation: Synthetic monitoring runs scripted user journeys (login, add to cart, checkout) every minute from multiple regions. It detects: broken flows that no current user is exercising, regional availability issues, performance degradation before user complaints, and issues that fall below alert thresholds. Tools: Datadog Synthetics, Checkly, Pingdom, AWS CloudWatch Synthetics.

questions.question: What is a Prometheus Alertmanager and how does alert routing work?

options.text: Alertmanager is a Grafana plugin that shows alerts on dashboards
Alertmanager receives alerts from Prometheus, deduplicates them, groups related alerts, and routes them to receivers (PagerDuty, Slack, email) based on routing rules
Alertmanager is a tool for writing PromQL alert rules
Alertmanager is the Prometheus UI for viewing current alert states

questions.explanation: Flow: Prometheus evaluates alerting rules (PromQL expressions) and sends firing alerts to Alertmanager. Alertmanager: (1) Deduplicates identical alerts. (2) Groups related alerts (e.g., all alerts from the same cluster in one message). (3) Routes based on labels (production alerts → PagerDuty, dev alerts → Slack). (4) Silences during maintenance windows.

questions.question: What is the USE method for performance analysis?

options.text: USE: Unified Service Engine — a method for consolidating monitoring tools
USE: Utilization, Saturation, Errors — for every resource (CPU, memory, disk, network), check these three metrics to systematically identify bottlenecks
USE: Uptime, Speed, Efficiency — the three pillars of performance
USE is a Datadog methodology for APM configuration

questions.explanation: The USE method (Brendan Gregg): for every resource, check: Utilization (how busy the resource is as a percentage), Saturation (the degree to which the resource has extra work it can't service — queue length), Errors (error events for that resource). Systematically applying USE to CPU, memory, disk I/O, and network quickly narrows down performance bottlenecks.
